findings.how_to_check: Run in Stata: count if wom & has_dmonth & hasml & cell==4. The count will be ~330,000, refuting the claim that group 4 is empty or near-empty.
findings.suggested_fix: Either amend the note in line 197 to state that group 4 is empty only for men (for women, group 4 contains records where the model produced a first name but lacked a surname in the full-name cell classification), or define a sex-specific cell variable where cell 4 reflects first-name missingness for women.
findings.title: Group 4 is claimed to be empty or near-empty under model-names-present restriction but contains ~330,000 records for women
findings.what_the_code_does: Line 150 defines 'gen byte hasml = (men & hm_f & hm_l) | (wom & hm_f)', requiring only first-name completeness for women. Line 197 writes to the report header that sections marked 'model names present' keep only records where the model produced every name scored, 'so no source is scored on an empty model name; group 4 is then empty or near-empty'. However, 'cell' is inherited from profile_names_build.do:47-53, where cell 4 is defined as 'disc & !ml_ok' with 'ml_ok = namefrst_ml!=\"\" & namelast_ml_ditto!=\"\"'. Women whose model first name is present but whose model surname is missing were assigned to cell 4 in profile_names_build.do, yet satisfy hasml in profile_names_jw.do. In the resulting table for women under hasml, group 4 is not empty; it contains over 330,000 records.
findings.why_it_matters: The generated report header directly contradicts the table printed beneath it. Readers are told group 4 is empty or near-empty and that no source is scored on an empty model name, but will see hundreds of thousands of observations in group 4 where the model first name is present, valid, and scored (~41% exact agreement and ~0.89 JW similarity). Labeling these valid first-name transcriptions under group 4 '(missing)' misrepresents their completeness.

findings.how_to_check: Run in Stata: count if wom & inrange(cell,1,4) & namefrst==fs_namefrst. The count will reveal millions of women in discordant cells who have identical first names across Ancestry and FamilySearch.
findings.suggested_fix: Clarify in line 197 that cells 0-4 are partitioned on full-name discordance (first name or surname) rather than first-name discordance alone.
findings.title: Discordant groups for women partition on full-name discordance rather than first-name discordance
findings.what_the_code_does: Lines 207-216 iterate over groups all, 0, disc, 1, 2, 3, 4 for women and evaluate first-name agreement (xf and jf). Line 197 defines the partition as: 'Cell 0 = Ancestry and FamilySearch agree; 1-4 = they disagree'. However, cell is inherited from profile_names_build.do:46 where disc is defined as '!(namefrst==fs_namefrst & namelast==fs_namelast)'. Consequently, records where Ancestry and FamilySearch agree on first name but disagree on surname are assigned to disc (and cells 1-4).
findings.why_it_matters: In a table specifically presenting first-name performance for women, a reader expects 'disc' and cells 1-4 to represent cases where Ancestry and FamilySearch disagreed on first name. Instead, millions of records in group disc have identical first names across Ancestry and FamilySearch, causing both sources to show high exact agreement (~53% and ~66%) within the ostensibly 'discordant' partition.

findings.how_to_check: Inspect MATCHING/results/profile_names_jw.md under '## Men, death month on profile, model names present: first name and surname' row '| 4 |'.
findings.suggested_fix: Check if r(N)==0 before formatting means, and print '-' or 'n/a' instead of formatting missing values as '.', or suppress the row if empty.
findings.title: Empty group 4 under men with model names present outputs Stata missing value dots across all 16 metric columns
findings.what_the_code_does: In lines 217-228, when cond is 'men&has_dmonth&hasml' and g is 4, count returns r(N)==0 because hasml requires both model names while cell 4 requires at least one model name missing. When quietly sum evaluates over 0 observations, r(mean) is missing (.), and string(100*r(mean), \"%5.1f\") and string(r(mean), \"%5.3f\") format it as '.'. The code writes '| 4 | 0 | . | . | ... | .' to the markdown file.
findings.why_it_matters: A published exhibit or documentation table containing raw Stata missing value dots '.' looks unhandled and can cause issues for automated markdown table parsers expecting numeric values.

findings.how_to_check: Run in Stata: count if strtrim(namefrst_ml)!=\"\" & cf_ml==\"\". If 0, no records are affected.
findings.suggested_fix: Evaluate fallback after normalization, or define cf_mf = cond(cf_ml==\"\", cf_anc, cf_ml).
findings.title: Fallback to Ancestry for ours+Anc is evaluated on raw strings while model presence is evaluated after normalization
findings.what_the_code_does: Lines 108-111 construct namefrst_mf and namelast_mf using 'fb_f = strtrim(namefrst_ml)==\"\"' and 'fb_l = strtrim(namelast_ml_ditto)==\"\"' before normalization. In contrast, lines 136-138 define model presence using 'hm_f = cf_ml!=\"\"' and 'hm_l = cl_ml!=\"\"' after pnorm. If a model transcription contains non-empty characters that normalize to empty (e.g. punctuation or noise), fallback to Ancestry is not triggered, yet the record is treated as missing under hasml.
findings.why_it_matters: If unparseable non-alphabetic strings occur in raw model transcriptions, ours+Anc fails to substitute Ancestry's name, leaving an empty normalized name that scores 0. In practice, model names in the dataset are predominantly cleaned or empty, making the numerical consequence negligible.

summary: The script MATCHING/profile_names_jw.do implements a rigorous Jaro-Winkler string similarity comparison between census transcriptions and FamilySearch profile names, correctly verifying exact agreement against prior benchmarks and guarding against missing-string equalities. The primary defect is in the newly added hasml specification for women, where group 4 is described in the markdown header as 'empty or near-empty' but actually contains over 300,000 records because cell 4 was defined using surname completeness while hasml for women requires only first-name completeness. Additionally, discordant cells 1-4 for women partition on full-name discordance rather than first-name discordance, misclassifying women with concordant first names into discordant cells.
